analysis.summary: Japan and Sweden meet in a decisive Group F finale with contrasting incentives: Japan (4 pts, +4 GD) need only a draw to advance as group runners-up, while Sweden (3 pts, 0 GD) must win to guarantee progression. Japan have impressed with a 2-2 draw vs Netherlands and a dominant 4-0 win over Tunisia, whereas Sweden beat Tunisia 5-1 but were then thrashed 5-1 by the Netherlands. This asymmetry in match stakes strongly shapes the tactical outlook, with Japan likely to defend compactly and Sweden forced to press aggressively for a goal.
analysis.home_form: Japan drew 2-2 with Netherlands on June 14 (twice coming from behind) then beat Tunisia 4-0 on June 20 (Ueda brace, Kamada and Ito also scoring). Four points from two games, goal difference +4. Key absentees: captain Wataru Endo (foot injury, retired from international football), Takefusa Kubo (knee, injured vs Netherlands), Kaoru Mitoma (hamstring, pre-tournament), Takumi Minamino (ACL, pre-tournament). Itakura Ko wearing the armband. Formation: 3-4-2-1 under Moriyasu with Ayase Ueda as lone striker, Kamada and Ito in the pockets, Doan and Nakamura as wing-backs.
analysis.away_form: Sweden beat Tunisia 5-1 on June 14 (Ayari brace, Isak assist, Gyokeres goal, Svanberg goal), then lost 5-1 to Netherlands on June 20. Three points, GD 0. Both Alexander Isak and Viktor Gyokeres are fit and available. Gustafsson Gudmundsson received a yellow card against Netherlands (not suspension-triggering at this stage). Formation: 3-5-2 under Graham Potter with Isak and Gyokeres up front, Ayari, Karlstrom, and Gudmundsson in midfield.
analysis.h2h: Limited head-to-head history. Japan lead the overall series with 2 wins, 2 draws, and 1 loss across five senior meetings, though all recent meetings since 1936 have been friendlies. Most recent meeting was a 1-1 friendly draw in May 2002. This is their first competitive senior international encounter. No meaningful historical pattern to extrapolate.
injuries_news: Japan: Wataru Endo (captain) ruled out of entire tournament with foot injury — retired from international football. Significant midfield and leadership loss.
Japan: Takefusa Kubo ruled out vs Sweden with knee injury sustained vs Netherlands in matchday 1.
Japan: Kaoru Mitoma (hamstring) and Takumi Minamino (ACL) ruled out pre-tournament — Japan without several attacking options.
Sweden: No confirmed injuries or suspensions. Isak and Gyokeres both fit and expected to start.
Sweden: Alexander Isak was managed for minutes during the week but is confirmed available.
key_factors: Incentive asymmetry: Japan need only a draw to qualify; Sweden must win. This structurally favors Japan's defensive setup and counter-attack strategy.

Japan's tactical discipline: Moriyasu's 3-4-2-1 is extremely hard to break down, built on narrow shape and rapid transitions. Sweden's 3-5-2 with two strikers will probe but may struggle vs packed Japan defense.

Sweden's attacking firepower: Isak (Newcastle) and Gyokeres (Sporting/Arsenal) form one of Europe's most dangerous strike partnerships. Even a disciplined Japan may not keep two clean sheets in the group stage.

Japan's key absences: Without Endo, Mitoma, Minamino, and Kubo, Japan lack width and creativity. This may limit their own attacking output, making a 1-0 or 1-1 scoreline more likely than a high-scoring game.
Venue: AT&T Stadium in Arlington has retractable roof and climate control — a fully enclosed environment removes heat/humidity as a factor. Both teams benefit equally from controlled conditions.
Rest: Both teams had their last match on June 20 (5 days' rest), so fatigue is not a differential factor.

Group context: Opta gives Sweden a 91.9% chance of advancing even with a draw, depending on goal difference vs third-place teams, so a draw might still allow both teams through. However, Sweden are seeking security and points.
Sweden's morale after 5-1 thrashing by Netherlands may affect their confidence but also their urgency to prove themselves.
